hypotheses.hypothesis: Across all coverage, mentions of 'LGBT' and 'gay rights' rose between 2006 and 2011 as public acceptance of homosexuality grew, which corresponds to Direction A.

Within coverage of same-sex marriage, religiously framed moral condemnation language such as 'sin' and 'abomination' declined between 2006 and 2011 as the debate shifted toward equality, which corresponds to Direction A.

Around 2006 coverage more often used the clinical-sounding term 'homosexuals', while by 2011 'gay people' and 'gay men and lesbians' had become more common, reflecting increasing acceptance, which corresponds to Direction A.
Within military policy coverage, framing around banning homosexuals from service was gradually replaced by framing around gay service members and repeal, which corresponds to Direction A.

Across all coverage, references to gay people being open about their sexuality, such as 'coming out' and 'openly gay', increased from 2006 to 2011, consistent with growing social acceptance and Direction A.

Across all New York Times coverage, references to family-centered values such as 'family values' and 'family first' become more frequent between 2006 and 2011, consistent with family rising in perceived importance.

Within coverage of the recession and jobs, language emphasizing families bearing the burden and relying on each other increases between 2006 and 2011, reflecting greater emphasis on family support during economic hardship.

Across all coverage, debates framed around individual lifestyle choices and divorce-era family structure give way to language about spending time together and family togetherness by 2011, indicating family becoming more central to personal life.

Within workplace and career coverage, the framing shifts from long hours and career advancement toward family-friendly policies and time with children by 2011, consistent with family taking greater priority.
Across all coverage, phrases about family routines and home life become more common between 2006 and 2011, suggesting a rise in the perceived importance of family in daily life.

Across all New York Times coverage, mentions of fraud-related vocabulary such as scam, swindle, and con artist rise between 2006 and 2011, reflecting a growing public expectation that others may take advantage.
Within coverage of the housing and financial crisis, language about victims being exploited by predatory lenders and fraudsters becomes more frequent between 2006 and 2011.
Coverage shifts from language presuming good faith in people toward language expressing suspicion and wariness of others over the period.
Within coverage of financial markets and investing, framing shifts from trusting advisers and firms toward describing investors as being preyed upon by schemes between 2006 and 2011.
Across all coverage, phrases signaling cooperative assumptions about other people decline in frequency between 2006 and 2011.

Across all New York Times coverage, references to fraud, scams, and distrust become more frequent between 2006 and 2011, consistent with a shift toward people feeling they need to be careful with others.
Within coverage of the financial crisis and Wall Street, language about deception and betrayal rises between 2006 and 2011, reflecting heightened wariness toward financial actors.
Around 2006, coverage leans on trust-affirming community language, while by 2011 it leans on vocabulary of scrutiny and caution, indicating a move toward wariness in dealing with people.

Within coverage of online life, early reporting emphasizes social connection and friendship, while later reporting emphasizes identity theft and phishing, suggesting people became more guarded in online interactions.
Across all New York Times coverage, language of cooperation and mutual goodwill becomes more frequent between 2006 and 2011, consistent with a shift toward perceiving most people as trustworthy.
As Americans grew less willing to express overt racial exclusion, New York Times coverage used the language of racial progress and colorblindness more often across all articles from 2006 to 2011.
Within coverage of housing and neighborhoods, references to explicit segregation practices declined between 2006 and 2011 as stated racial exclusion became less socially acceptable.
Coverage shifted from framing racial exclusion as a live problem of overt bias toward framing race relations through the lens of a post-racial or diversity-celebrating narrative.
Within articles about neighborhoods and integration, the framing moved from fears of white flight and resistance to newcomers toward descriptions of diverse, mixed neighborhoods.
Across all coverage, mentions of openly racist neighbor complaints and similar exclusionary attitudes became less frequent between 2006 and 2011.
